question: Can an optimizer for neural networks trained through differentiable physics balance ordinary parameter-space gradients against full physics-space inversion, correcting small physical modes without the neuron-saturating updates of Gauss-Newton?

key_findings.claim: Half-inverse gradients interpolate spectrally between gradient descent and Gauss-Newton by applying an inverse square root of the stacked network-solver Jacobian to the output-space loss gradient.
key_findings.evidence: For the paper's rectangular-SVD convention J=U Lambda V^T and J^kappa=V Lambda^kappa U^T, kappa=1 recovers J^T g, kappa=-1 recovers the pseudoinverse update, and kappa=-1/2 defines HIG. The batch construction stacks all examples before a single SVD, so it solves a coupled batch update rather than averaging independently preconditioned gradients.

key_findings.claim: The choice kappa=-1/2 is a symmetry-motivated empirical compromise, while Appendix A's claimed geometric support is dimensionally invalid as printed and supplies neither an optimality theorem nor a convergence guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: The main text chooses the midpoint by saying the burden of physical and network scaling is distributed equally, and the sole exponent ablation is one nonlinear-oscillator setup where negative exponents outperform positive ones and kappa=-1/2 is best. In Appendix A, however, Equation 6's rectangular convention J^kappa=V Lambda^kappa U^T makes Equation 14's J^(3/4) theta and Equation 16's product J^(1/4)J^(3/4) nonconformable; the displayed factorization silently changes the first factor to V Lambda^(1/4) V^T. The conclusion then prints -J^(1/2)g instead of HIG's -J^(-1/2)g. A dimensionally valid reviewer-derived parameter seminorm would use ||Lambda^(3/4) V^T Delta theta||, equivalently the metric V Lambda^(3/2) V^T, but that repair is not the authors' proof. Appendix C also calls the best kappa-ablation curve beta=-0.5 in prose, whereas Figure 12b and the next sentence identify kappa=-0.5. No global descent, generalization, convergence, or exponent-optimality theorem is supplied.

key_findings.claim: On the nonlinear-oscillator benchmark, the selected HIG run reaches lower reported test loss than Adam and the best stable Gauss-Newton run while avoiding the toy example's two diagnosed pathologies.
key_findings.evidence: The ill-conditioned toy visualization attributes Adam's failure to neglect of the down-scaled output coordinate and Gauss-Newton's failure to tanh-neuron saturation; HIG fits both coordinates without that collapse. For the two-mass quartic oscillator, the plotted best runs end near 10^-4 for Adam, 10^-6 for stable Gauss-Newton, and 10^-7 for HIG, with HIG and Gauss-Newton surpassing Adam after roughly three wall-clock minutes. These are selected single curves without uncertainty estimates.

key_findings.claim: The Poisson experiment is a counterexample to any blanket wall-clock-superiority claim: direct Adam is faster in absolute time, while HIG mainly shows greater progress per expensive update and can improve an Adam-pretrained solution.
key_findings.evidence: On the 8x8 Poisson problem, the paper explicitly says Adam converges faster in wall-clock time because each HIG update performs a large SVD. HIG has a steeper per-iteration curve and continues reducing error from an Adam checkpoint; conversely, Adam initialized from a HIG solution moves to a worse-loss regime. The benchmark generates right-hand sides online and has no separate held-out test set.

key_findings.claim: On the quantum-control task, HIG reaches the numerical-solver accuracy floor faster than Adam and learns both low- and high-energy error components more evenly.
key_findings.evidence: A three-layer tanh controller maps randomized superpositions of the first two excited states to 384 dipole-control values for a modified Crank-Nicolson evolution. The reported fidelity loss approaches about 10^-6, identified as the pure-physics discretization floor. Energy-resolved loss curves show Adam first reduces low-energy modes while HIG reduces low- and high-energy components together; an appendix CNN experiment also favors the best HIG run over the best Adam run.

key_findings.claim: The advertised linear scaling in network parameters hides the dominant quadratic dependence on both batch size and physical-state dimension, with very large measured time and memory premiums.
key_findings.evidence: The stated SVD cost is O(|theta| b^2 |y|^2). Appendix tables report, for example, 3.56 GB and 13.8 seconds per HIG Poisson update versus 1.3 MB and 0.011 seconds for Adam, approximately 1,250 times slower per update; nonlinear-oscillator HIG at batch 128 uses 2.64 GB versus Adam's 22.2 MB at batch 512; quantum HIG at batch 16 uses 5.039 GB.

key_findings.claim: The public artifact implements the inverse-square-root mechanism but does not exactly instantiate several paper specifications or provide end-to-end result verification.
key_findings.evidence: Repository commit 08d38820054569db869c5f5c0e4b20bd2a044e42 contains TensorFlow 2.5 scripts for the three physical systems and its Python files pass syntax compilation. However, its SVD helper cuts singular values below rcond times the largest singular value whereas page 5 describes an absolute tau cutoff; the Poisson script uses hidden widths 64-128-64 instead of the paper's 64-256-64; and oscillator HIG, GN, and Adam scripts use seeds 22, 28, and 1, respectively, changing both generated datasets and initialization. It ships no raw result files, checkpoints, tests, toy script, quantum CNN script, or scripts for four of the seven oscillator baselines, and its Poisson plot hard-codes [local-artifact-root]/phi/.

method.core_idea: Partially invert the singular spectrum of the complete network-plus-physics Jacobian so small physical modes receive more weight than under backpropagation but less explosive amplification than under a full pseudoinverse.
method.mechanism: For each mini-batch, differentiate physical outputs with respect to every trainable parameter, flatten and vertically stack the per-example Jacobians, flatten the output-space loss gradient, and compute a truncated thin SVD. Replace each retained singular value sigma by sigma^(-1/2), map the output gradient through V Sigma^(-1/2) U^T, reshape the resulting parameter vector, and apply it through SGD with learning rate eta. Singular modes below tau are removed. The paper also defines a general exponent kappa spanning gradient descent at 1 and Gauss-Newton at -1, plus an ablated maximum-singular-value prefactor beta.
assumptions: The simulator and network are differentiable enough for a first-order Jacobian to describe useful local output changes.
A squared-L2 output objective is the main derivational setting, although the quantum experiment uses a fidelity loss with an additional correction.
The stacked Jacobian's singular modes meaningfully separate physically important scales from numerical noise.
A problem-specific truncation threshold can be chosen from pure-physics solve accuracy without removing important small-scale modes.
The SVD is computationally feasible for the product of mini-batch size and physical output dimension.
Any geometric interpretation requires a dimensionally valid parameter-space metric and remains only local under rank deficiency, truncation, changing Jacobians, and finite update sizes.
The simplified pseudoinverse Gauss-Newton account assumes full rank on an unconstrained or suitably reparameterized accessible manifold.

techniques.role: Raises retained singular values to a tunable exponent and selects -1/2 between transpose-gradient and pseudoinverse updates.
Couples all examples in one spectral solve instead of averaging independently computed sample gradients.
Suppresses modes judged to be numerical noise before inverse-root amplification.
Separates quantum error into low- and high-energy components to diagnose which physical scales each optimizer learns.
Initializes HIG from an Adam solution and vice versa to test whether their terminal regions are mutually reachable.
Motivates a Jacobian-induced intermediate geometry, although the paper's rectangular-matrix proof is dimensionally invalid as printed.

evaluations.setting: Ill-conditioned two-output sinusoid toy regression with a seven-unit tanh hidden layer
evaluations.metric: Loss, output trajectory, and across-input neuron-output variance
evaluations.result: HIG fits the down-scaled coordinate while Adam stalls and avoids the neuron saturation observed for Gauss-Newton
evaluations.baseline: Adam and truncated Gauss-Newton under gamma=1 and gamma=0.01

evaluations.setting: Two coupled nonlinear oscillators, 96 RK4 control steps, 4,096 train and 4,096 test samples
evaluations.metric: Average test L2 loss against wall-clock time
evaluations.result: Selected HIG reaches about 10^-7 versus about 10^-6 for stable Gauss-Newton and 10^-4 for Adam
evaluations.baseline: SGD, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop, Adam, and Gauss-Newton

evaluations.setting: Online 8x8 Poisson inversion with a dense tanh network
evaluations.metric: Physics residual loss per wall-clock time and iteration
evaluations.result: Adam wins direct wall-clock convergence; HIG improves more per update and reduces loss further after Adam pretraining
evaluations.baseline: Adam, direct HIG, and cross-optimizer continuation

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional quantum dipole control with 384 differentiable time steps and 1,024 train/test states
evaluations.metric: Infidelity loss, wall-clock convergence, and low/high energy components
evaluations.result: HIG approaches the approximately 10^-6 solver floor faster and reduces energy components more uniformly

evaluations.setting: Quantum dipole control with a six-layer convolutional controller
evaluations.metric: Test loss over wall-clock time across hyperparameter sweeps
evaluations.result: Best reported HIG setting eta=0.7, batch 16, tau=10^-4 outperforms best Adam eta=0.0002, batch 256

evaluations.setting: Nonlinear-oscillator ablations over beta, kappa, and tau
evaluations.result: Beta has little effect, negative kappa values are much better than positive ones with -1/2 best in the shown sweep, and HIG remains stable at tau values where Gauss-Newton diverges
evaluations.baseline: Generalized fractional updates including gradient descent and Gauss-Newton endpoints

limitations: The exponent -1/2 is motivated by symmetry and one task-specific ablation; the paper does not prove it optimal or establish convergence, monotonic descent, or generalization.

Appendix A's geometric argument is not valid as printed for a rectangular Jacobian: its proposed seminorm and fractional-power product are dimensionally nonconformable under Equation 6's convention, before accounting for null spaces, truncation, Jacobian drift, or finite steps.

The appendix concludes with -J^(1/2)g rather than HIG's -J^(-1/2)g, and Appendix C mislabels the best kappa=-0.5 ablation curve as beta=-0.5 in prose; the main definition, Figure 12b, and code disambiguate both errors.
Exact Jacobian construction and SVD scale quadratically in batch size and physical-state dimension, producing orders-of-magnitude time and memory overhead even on 8x8 or 16-point systems.
All benchmark systems, grids, networks, and datasets are small; there is no chaotic long-horizon system, high-resolution PDE, operator-learning model, transformer, or million-parameter demonstration.
Main curves are the runs with best final test loss after method-specific searches, which uses the test set for model selection and does not preserve a clean held-out estimate.
No repeated-run statistics, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests accompany the selected curves.
The claimed broad hyperparameter search is only partially documented through example plots and selected settings, so its budget and fairness cannot be reconstructed.
The Poisson task has no distinct test set, and direct Adam is faster in wall-clock time despite the paper's broad abstract-level speed claim.
Absolute singular-value truncation is unit- and scale-dependent; the released implementation instead uses a relative cutoff, leaving the paper's precise algorithm ambiguous.
The public code's differing seeds, Poisson architecture mismatch, omitted experiment scripts, and absence of raw results/checkpoints prevent exact figure reproduction from the release alone.
failure_modes: A too-small tau inverse-amplifies numerical or poorly linearized modes into destructive parameter updates; a too-large tau deletes the small physical modes HIG is meant to preserve.
Increasing batch size can add nearly dependent Jacobian rows, worsening conditioning even while providing a better joint batch direction.
When batch-times-output dimension grows, explicit Jacobian storage or SVD becomes infeasible before parameter count itself is limiting.
Strong nonlinearity or an update outside the local linear regime invalidates the SVD-based output-change prediction and can still saturate neurons.
Rank-deficient or constrained problems make the simplified Gauss-Newton inverse and seminorm geometry non-unique without a carefully specified pseudoinverse and accessible manifold.
Changing physical units or globally rescaling outputs changes an absolute tau cutoff and can change which modes survive.
Selecting hyperparameters by terminal test loss can favor noisy late improvements and overstate out-of-sample performance.
A task where first-order updates are cheap and adequate, as in the direct Poisson run, can erase HIG's per-iteration advantage in wall-clock comparisons.
reusable_insights: Diagnose differentiable-physics training in the singular basis of the composite network-solver Jacobian rather than attributing all conditioning to the neural network.
Treat a mini-batch spectral solve as a coupled multi-example optimization object, not as a drop-in replacement for averaged stochastic gradients.
Report convergence both per iteration and per wall-clock time because sophisticated preconditioners can reverse their ranking between the two axes.
Use mode-resolved physical errors to verify that an optimizer improves hard small-scale modes rather than only reducing aggregate loss.
Calibrate spectral truncation against independent solver accuracy, then stress-test both smaller and larger thresholds.
Run optimizer-continuation experiments to distinguish optimization barriers from representational limits.
Hold data, initialization, tuning budget, and checkpoint selection fixed across optimizer comparisons, and preserve every run rather than only the best curve.
Specify whether an SVD threshold is absolute or relative to the largest singular value; the distinction changes scale behavior and reproducibility.
open_questions: Can inverse-root Jacobian-vector products be approximated matrix-free with randomized Krylov, Nyström, or block-diagonal methods while retaining HIG's physical-mode behavior?
Is there an adaptive rule for kappa and tau with a descent or trust-region guarantee rather than task-specific sweeps?
How does HIG compare under matched compute and tuning budgets with modern natural-gradient, Nyström-Newton, Shampoo/SOAP, and quasi-Newton methods?
Do the gains persist on high-resolution, chaotic, stiff, or long-horizon simulators where the composite Jacobian changes sharply?
What population behavior follows from coupling all examples in one SVD, and how does it change gradient noise or implicit regularization?
Can the local seminorm interpretation be made rigorous for rectangular, rank-deficient, truncated Jacobians with a changing accessible manifold?
Would relative or energy-aware mode thresholds preserve unit invariance better than the paper's stated absolute tau?
Do matched-seed reruns and a validation-selected protocol reproduce the reported oscillator and quantum rankings with uncertainty estimates?

competitive_landscape.title: Scale-invariant Learning by Physics Inversion
competitive_landscape.relationship: The direct predecessor replaces gradients through a physical process with updates from a scale-invariant inverse-problem solver and targets the same differentiable-physics conditioning problem.
competitive_landscape.difference: It requires a problem-specific physics inversion procedure, whereas HIG constructs a generic fractional inverse from the complete network-solver Jacobian; HIG is less fully scale-normalizing but tries to protect network capacity from full inverse updates.

competitive_landscape.title: Achieving High Accuracy with PINNs via Energy Natural Gradients
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later physics-specific method also changes the optimization geometry to counter poor conditioning, using a Hessian-induced energy metric for PINNs and deep Ritz models.
competitive_landscape.difference: Energy natural gradient is derived from the variational energy and projects a function-space Newton direction onto the model tangent space; HIG acts on the empirical composite simulator Jacobian and was evaluated on differentiable control/inversion rather than PINN residual training.

competitive_landscape.title: Challenges in Training PINNs: A Loss Landscape Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: This later work directly ties differential operators to ill-conditioned physics-learning losses and introduces Nyström Newton-CG as a scalable second-order remedy.
competitive_landscape.difference: NNCG uses randomized low-rank Hessian information and conjugate gradients after Adam on PINNs, avoiding HIG's exact stacked-Jacobian SVD; its benchmarks and objective class are adjacent rather than a direct differentiable-simulator replication.

competitive_landscape.title: Gauss-Newton Natural Gradient Descent for Physics-Informed Computational Fluid Dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: This later physics-specific optimizer derives a function-space Gauss-Newton natural gradient for PINN fluid dynamics and gives it a matrix-free implementation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its geometry comes from the PINN residual and integral discretization and targets full Gauss-Newton dynamics without an explicit stacked-Jacobian SVD; HIG instead half-inverts the empirical network-simulator Jacobian to moderate unstable inverse modes in differentiable control and inversion.

competitive_landscape.title: SOAP: Improving and Stabilizing Shampoo using Adam
competitive_landscape.relationship: SOAP is a current scalable inverse-root preconditioner that combines Shampoo eigenspaces with Adam-like second moments and is relevant to HIG's goal of balancing curvature correction with stable neural training.
competitive_landscape.difference: SOAP preconditions parameter matrices from gradient statistics and scales to large language models; it neither uses a physical solver Jacobian nor promises output-mode correction, but its amortized eigendecompositions avoid HIG's batch-output SVD bottleneck.

competitive_landscape.title: Dual Natural Gradient Descent for Scalable Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: D-NGD is a later physics-learning optimizer that computes an exact Gauss-Newton/natural-gradient direction in the usually smaller residual space and offers dense or Nyström-preconditioned iterative solvers.
competitive_landscape.difference: It targets PINN residual classes and full Gauss-Newton geometry, adds geodesic acceleration, and reports networks up to 12.8 million parameters; HIG uses a half inverse to control full-inverse instability but retains an explicit SVD whose practical scale is much smaller.

competitive_landscape.title: PDE-aware Optimizer for Physics-informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: This later first-order alternative addresses stiffness and gradient misalignment by adapting updates from per-sample PDE-residual gradient variance.
competitive_landscape.difference: It avoids explicit curvature matrices and reports lower overhead than second-order methods, but is tailored to PINN residual balancing and does not spectrally restore attenuated modes of a differentiable forward simulator as HIG does.

competitive_landscape.title: Curvature-Aware Optimization for High-Accuracy Physics-Informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: This current physics-learning study evaluates scalable natural-gradient, self-scaling BFGS, and Broyden optimizers on high-accuracy PDE and stiff-ODE problems, including batched training.
competitive_landscape.difference: It attacks curvature with matrix-free natural gradients and quasi-Newton updates across broader PINN benchmarks, whereas HIG uses a fixed fractional inverse of the complete differentiable-simulator Jacobian and is demonstrated only with small explicit SVDs.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents half-inverse gradients as a generic optimizer for joint neural-network and differentiable-physics objectives, using the kappa=-1/2 fractional inverse of the complete network-solver Jacobian to balance ordinary gradient descent against full Gauss-Newton inversion.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Equations 5-7 define the spectral interpolation and coupled batch update, while the selected oscillator and quantum runs outperform the paper's first-order baselines and stable Gauss-Newton runs; the Poisson experiment instead favors Adam in direct wall-clock time. The public implementation instantiates the inverse-root update but differs from the paper in cutoff convention, one architecture, comparison seeds, and experiment coverage.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is algorithmic and diagnostic: applying a fixed fractional inverse to the complete network-physics Jacobian makes the conflict between parameter-space learning and physics-space inversion explicit and differs from the authors' solver-specific predecessor. The kappa=-1/2 midpoint remains heuristic, however, and Appendix A does not provide valid geometric support as printed because its rectangular fractional-power expressions are dimensionally nonconformable and its concluding exponent has the wrong sign. Exact SVD cost, small selected-curve experiments, and incomplete artifact reproduction prevent a general scalable-optimizer conclusion, especially beside later matrix-free natural-gradient and curvature-aware physics optimizers.
